lessons.title: Lesson 1: Which tasks pay to mechanize
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the tasks on your farm that pay to mechanize.
This lesson builds toward: Given the tasks on your farm, you will identify which tasks pay to mechanize, giving a reason for each: timeliness, labour, losses or volume.
Mechanization means using tools and machines, from improved hand tools and animal traction to tractors and motorized machines, to do farm work. FAO stresses choosing what fits the farm, the people and the place. A machine pays when it earns or saves more than it costs.
Tasks that often pay: land preparation, when ploughing or ripping on time after the first rains lets you plant on time; threshing and shelling, where a machine does in hours what takes many people days and loses less grain on the ground; transport of harvest and inputs; pumping water; and processing such as grating cassava or milling. Tasks that pay less: small plots, work that is cheap and quick by hand, or tasks you do only once a year for a few hours.
Ask four questions about each task. Timeliness: does doing it late cut the yield? Labour: is labour short or costly at that time? Losses: does doing it by hand lose crop? Volume: is there enough work to keep a machine busy? Then compare the cost by hand and by machine. Example (figures are only an example): ploughing 1 hectare by hand takes 25 person-days at GHS 50 = GHS 1,250, while hiring a tractor costs GHS 600 per hectare.
Step by step:
- List every big task on your farm through the year.
- For each, ask: timeliness, labour, losses, volume.
- Work out the cost by hand: person-days x daily wage.
- Find the cost by machine: hire rate x hectares.
- Mark the tasks where the machine costs less or earns more.
Words to know:
- Mechanization: using tools and machines, from better hand tools to tractors, to do farm work.
- Timeliness: doing a task at the right time, such as planting soon after the rains start.
- Person-day: the work one person does in one day.
Official sources:
- FAO: Sustainable agricultural mechanization (from hand tools to motorized equipment)
- FAO and African Union Commission: Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization: A Framework for Africa (2018)
Try it now: List five big tasks on your farm. For each, answer the four questions (timeliness, labour, losses, volume) and compare the cost by hand with the cost by machine. Circle the two tasks that pay most to mechanize.
You can now pick the tasks on your farm that pay to mechanize and say why.

check.q: Why does ploughing on time often pay?
options: Tractors are cheaper in the dry season
Planting on time after the rains can raise yield
It makes the field look neat
check.why: Timeliness matters: late planting often cuts yield.

check.q: Shelling 2 tonnes of maize by hand takes 20 person-days at NGN 4,000. A sheller service costs NGN 50,000. Which is cheaper?
check.why: Hand shelling costs 20 x 4,000 = NGN 80,000, more than NGN 50,000.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Hiring versus owning: a worked cost comparison
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the cost of owning and hiring and find the break-even area.
This lesson builds toward: Given the price, running costs and hire rate of a machine, you will calculate the yearly cost of owning, the cost of hiring and the break-even area, with the sums correct and a clear hire or buy decision.
Owning a machine has fixed costs you pay every year even if it never moves: the loss in value over its life (depreciation), the interest on a loan or what the money could have earned elsewhere, insurance, and a shed. It also has running costs per hectare: fuel, oil, repairs and the operator. Hiring has one cost: the hire rate per hectare.
Worked example for a tractor and plough in Nigeria (all figures are examples only; use real quotes and your lender's real rate): price NGN 30,000,000, worth NGN 6,000,000 after 10 years, so depreciation = (30,000,000 - 6,000,000) / 10 = NGN 2,400,000 a year. Loan interest (example) NGN 1,800,000 a year, insurance and shed NGN 600,000. Fixed costs = NGN 4,800,000 a year. Running costs = NGN 25,000 per hectare. Hire rate = NGN 60,000 per hectare.
Each hectare you plough with your own tractor saves 60,000 - 25,000 = NGN 35,000 compared with hiring. Break-even area = fixed costs / saving per hectare = 4,800,000 / 35,000 = about 137 hectares a year. A farmer with 10 hectares should hire; owning only pays if the tractor also works on neighbours' farms. Also weigh what numbers miss: owning means you plough on time, while hiring means no loan and no repairs. Leasing and pay-as-you-go deals are other options; read every contract fully and ask a trusted adviser.
Step by step:
- Depreciation per year = (price - value at the end) / years of use.
- Add interest, insurance and shed: these are fixed costs per year.
- Add fuel, oil, repairs and operator per hectare: running costs.
- Saving per hectare = hire rate - running costs.
- Break-even area = fixed costs / saving per hectare.
- Compare with your hectares and decide; note timeliness and risk.
Words to know:
- Depreciation: the value a machine loses each year as it ages.
- Fixed costs: costs you pay each year whether or not the machine works.
- Break-even area: the hectares a year at which owning costs the same as hiring.
Official sources:
- FAO: Hire services as a business (sustainable agricultural mechanization)
- FAO and African Union Commission: Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization: A Framework for Africa (2018)
Try it now: Get real quotes for one machine you are thinking of (price, expected life and value at the end, running costs and the local hire rate). Work out its fixed costs per year, the saving per hectare and the break-even area, and write whether you should hire or buy.
You can now compare the cost of owning and hiring a machine and find the break-even area.

check.q: A sheller costs GHS 20,000 and is worth GHS 4,000 after 8 years. What is its depreciation per year?
Fixed costs are KES 300,000 a year and owning saves KES 6,000 per hectare. What is the break-even area?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Tractor-hire and app-based services
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Book a hire service and check the work before you pay.
This lesson builds toward: When you hire a tractor or machine service, you will agree the price, area, date and quality in advance and check the work before paying, measuring the field and getting a receipt.
You can hire machines from a neighbour or tractor owner, a cooperative or farmer group, a government or private hire centre, or an app-based service. Hello Tractor is one example: farmers book tractor services through its mobile app or web app or through booking agents (extension and field agents who book for farmers), and tractor owners use it to track their tractors and fuel by GPS. It also offers pay-as-you-go deals to help people own tractors. The company says it works in more than 20 African countries, including Nigeria; check what is available in your area.
Tractors go first where there is a lot of work in one place. Booking together with neighbours, so the tractor can do many farms in one trip, makes it more likely to come on time.
Before work starts, agree in writing or by message: the price per acre or hectare, how the area will be measured, the date, the depth and type of work, and who pays for fuel. Measure the field yourself, with a tape or a phone GPS app. After the work, check it: right depth, no strips missed, the whole field done. Pay only after checking, through the official app, mobile money or with a receipt. Never pay a stranger in advance outside the official app, and never share PINs or codes.
Step by step:
- Choose a service: neighbour, group, hire centre or app (for example Hello Tractor).
- Book early, together with neighbours if you can.
- Agree price, area measurement, date, depth and fuel in advance.
- Measure the field yourself.
- Check the work: depth, no missed strips, whole field.
- Pay after checking; get a receipt or app record; never share PINs.
Words to know:
- Booking agent: a person who books machine services for farmers, often using an app.
- Pay-as-you-go (PAYG): paying for something in small amounts over time while you use it, until you own it.
- Hire rate: the price the service charges, often per acre or per hectare.
Official sources:
- Hello Tractor: tractor booking by app, web or booking agent; fleet tracking; pay-as-you-go ownership
- FAO: Hire services as a business (sustainable agricultural mechanization)
Try it now: Find two hire services near you (a tractor owner, a group, a hire centre or an app). Ask each for the price per hectare, how they measure the area, when they can come, and how you pay. Write a short booking message that sets out all the terms.
You can now book a tractor or machine service with clear terms and check the work before you pay.

check.q: When should you pay for tractor ploughing?
options: After checking the work and the area, with a receipt or app record
Before the tractor arrives, in cash to whoever calls
Half to a stranger by text
check.why: Checking first and getting a record protects you from poor work and scams.

check.q: How can you make a hired tractor more likely to come on time?
options: Book alone for a tiny plot
Pay a stranger extra in advance
check.why: Many farms in one place make the trip worth it for the tractor owner.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Running machines and a service business

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Small machines for smallholders
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a small machine that fits your task and your area.
This lesson builds toward: Given a farm task and your local market, you will choose a small machine that fits the task, the volume of work and the spare parts and mechanics nearby, listing at least four checks before buying.
Not every farm needs a four-wheel tractor. A two-wheel tractor (power tiller) can plough, rotavate, pump water and pull a trailer on small plots. A motorized maize sheller or a multi-crop thresher (for rice, sorghum, millet, beans or soybeans) saves days of labour and loses less grain. A motorized knapsack sprayer or mistblower covers more ground than a hand sprayer. Other examples are cassava graters, rice reapers and chaff cutters for fodder.
Before buying, check: Is there enough work, on your farm and your neighbours', to keep it busy? Can a nearby mechanic repair it, and are spare parts sold near you? Does the dealer train you and give a warranty? Can it be moved between farms? Can the people who will use it, including women and young people, operate it safely? FAO has published a catalogue of machines suited to women farmers.
Sprayers: use only pesticides registered in your country, as the label says, with protective equipment. In Kenya check the Pest Control Products Board list; in Nigeria, NAFDAC. A motorized sprayer puts out more chemical faster, so set it up (calibrate it) as its manual says before each season.
Step by step:
- Name the task and how many hectares or tonnes a year.
- Choose the machine type for that task.
- Check spare parts and a mechanic near you.
- Ask the dealer about training and warranty.
- Check it can be moved and safely used by your operators.
- For sprayers: registered pesticides only, label and protective equipment.
Words to know:
- Two-wheel tractor: a small walk-behind tractor, also called a power tiller, that pulls tools and powers pumps.
- Thresher: a machine that separates grain from the plant stalks.
- Calibrate: set a sprayer so it puts out the right amount, as its manual and the pesticide label say.
Official sources:
- FAO: Sustainable agricultural mechanization (from hand tools to motorized equipment)
- Pest Control Products Board (Kenya): registered products
- National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC, Nigeria)
Try it now: Pick one task from Lesson 1. Choose a small machine for it and visit or phone a dealer. Ask the price, where spare parts and repairs are, what training and warranty they give, and how much work it can do in a day. Write the answers down.
You can now choose a small machine that fits your task, your area and the people who will use it.

check.q: Which machine fits ploughing and pumping on small plots?
check.why: A power tiller ploughs small plots and can drive a pump.

check.q: The cheapest sheller has no spare parts or mechanic within 200 km. What is the risk?
options: When it breaks, it may stand idle for weeks
It will use too little fuel
check.why: A machine with no nearby parts or repairs can be idle when you need it most.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Safety and maintenance logs
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Run a machine safely and keep its maintenance log.
This lesson builds toward: Before and after each use of a machine, you will carry out the safety checks and record the work and maintenance in a logbook, with no safety rule skipped and every entry dated.
Machines can kill or maim in seconds. Tractor overturns, people falling under wheels, and clothes caught in spinning shafts are common causes of death on farms. The ILO publishes a code of practice on safe tractor use. The main rules: only trained adults operate machines; no children near working machines; no passengers on the tractor or implements; use the roll-over protection and seat belt where fitted; go slowly and straight across slopes and away from ditches; keep all guards in place, especially on the power take-off (PTO) shaft; and wear close-fitting clothes with hair tied back.
Threshers and shellers: never put your hand into the feed opening or a blockage. Stop the engine and wait for all parts to stop before clearing it. Protect ears and lungs from noise and dust. Refuel only with the engine off and cool, with no smoking. Keep a first-aid kit and a phone nearby.
A machine that is looked after lasts longer and breaks down less in the busy season. Do daily checks before work: engine oil, fuel, water or coolant, air filter, tyres, loose nuts and bolts, and grease points. Service it by the hours on its meter as the manual says. Keep a logbook with: date, hours, job and hectares or tonnes, fuel, repairs and parts, cost, and the operator's name. The log shows the real running cost per hectare.
Step by step:
- Trained adult operator only; no children, no passengers.
- Guards on, roll-over protection and seat belt used where fitted.
- Go slowly on slopes; keep away from ditches.
- Stop the engine and wait before clearing any blockage.
- Daily checks: oil, fuel, coolant, air filter, tyres, bolts, grease.
- Write each day's work, fuel, repairs and costs in the logbook.
Words to know:
- PTO (power take-off) shaft: a spinning shaft on a tractor that drives tools; it can catch clothes and kill.
- Roll-over protection: a frame over the driver's seat that protects them if the tractor tips over.
- Logbook: a book where you record every job, fuel, repair and cost for a machine.
Official sources:
- ILO: Safe construction and operation of tractors (code of practice)
Try it now: Make a one-page safety checklist for one machine you use or hire, and a logbook page with columns for date, hours, job, hectares or tonnes, fuel, repairs and parts, cost, and operator. Fill in one line from a real or example job.
You can now run a machine with the key safety rules and keep a maintenance log that shows its true running cost.

check.q: A thresher is blocked. What do you do?
options: Push the crop in with your hand while it runs
Ask a child to pull it out
Stop the engine, wait for all parts to stop, then clear it
check.why: Moving parts can take a hand in a second; only clear a stopped machine.

check.q: Which belongs in a machine logbook?
options: Date, hours, job, fuel, repairs and cost
Only the colour of the machine
check.why: These records show the real running cost and when service is due.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Starting a mechanization service business
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page plan for a machine hire service.
This lesson builds toward: Given a machine and the farms around you, you will write a one-page plan for a mechanization hire service, with services, customers, price, costs, break-even and risks.
Many hire services are run by farmers who bought a machine for their own farm and then offer it to neighbours, for cash or in exchange for other work or crops. FAO and the African Union's framework for mechanization in Africa see young people running hire services as a key way to bring machines to smallholders. FAO also publishes a training manual on hire services as a business.
A one-page plan answers: What services, in which seasons (ploughing, shelling, threshing, transport, pumping)? Who are the customers, and how many hectares or tonnes in total? What price, and how does it compare with other services? What are the costs (fixed per year and running per hectare, from Lessons 2 and 5)? What is the break-even? How will you take bookings and payment (deposits, mobile money, receipts)? Who is the operator, and are they trained? What are the risks: breakdowns in the peak season, unpaid jobs, accidents, theft? How will you reduce them (maintenance, written terms, insurance, a GPS tracker)?
Example for a power tiller service in Senegal or Burkina Faso (all figures are examples only): fixed costs XOF 600,000 a year, running costs XOF 15,000 per hectare, price XOF 35,000 per hectare. Break-even = 600,000 / (35,000 - 15,000) = 30 hectares. With 50 hectares booked, profit = 50 x 20,000 - 600,000 = XOF 400,000. Group nearby farms together to cut travel, and add off-season work such as shelling and transport. Finance options include loans, leases and pay-as-you-go deals: read every contract fully and ask a trusted adviser.
Step by step:
- List your services and seasons.
- List customers and total hectares or tonnes.
- Set a price that covers cost per hectare plus a margin; compare with others.
- Work out break-even: fixed costs / (price - running cost per hectare).
- Plan bookings, operator, payment and records.
- List the risks and how you will reduce each one.
Words to know:
- Hire service: a business that does farm work with its machines for other farmers, for a fee.
- Margin: the part of the price left after costs.
- Off-season work: jobs a machine can do outside the main season, such as transport or shelling.
Official sources:
- FAO: Hire services as a business (sustainable agricultural mechanization)
- FAO: Hire services as a business enterprise (training manual)
- FAO and African Union Commission: Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization: A Framework for Africa (2018)
- Hello Tractor: tractor booking by app, web or booking agent; fleet tracking; pay-as-you-go ownership
Try it now: Final task: make your hire-versus-buy decision sheet for one machine and task. If owning only pays with neighbours' work, add a one-page hire service plan: services, customers and hectares, price, costs, break-even, bookings and payment, and the main risks.
You can now plan a machine hire service with prices, costs, break-even and risks.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Task choice No reason given for mechanizing the task. The task is chosen with reasons (timeliness, labour, losses or volume) and a cost by hand. Compares two or more tasks and explains why this one pays most. Cost comparison Fixed or running costs missing, or the sums are wrong. Depreciation, fixed costs, running costs, hire cost and break-even area correct, with a clear decision. Uses real quotes and notes timeliness and risk beside the numbers. Machine and hire checks No checks on parts, repairs or the hire service. Lists checks on parts, mechanic, training and warranty, or on the hire service's terms. Has asked a dealer or hire service and records the answers. Safety and maintenance No safety rules or no logbook. Key safety rules and a logbook with date, hours, job, fuel, repairs and cost. Names who is trained to operate and when the first service is due. Decision and business plan No decision, or a buy decision with no plan to keep the machine busy. Clear decision; if buying, a one-page hire plan with services, customers, price, costs, break-even and risks. Shows the plan still works with 20% fewer hectares booked, or says what would change. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Fixed costs are XOF 400,000 a year, running costs XOF 10,000 per hectare and the price XOF 30,000 per hectare. What is the break-even area?
Which step lowers the travel cost of a tractor hire service?
options: Taking jobs far apart on the same day
check.why: Doing nearby farms together saves fuel and time on the road.
